yarn-troppo.meaning: All facts survive (1791, 70 mph, 1789–1797, the whisky barrel, the Clinton disclaimer, the magnolia and sequoia), with asides that hang off them: "Imagine running the joint from your back paddock." One small change: "they've gathered up the whole Canadian hemlock to keep it" adds 'whole'.
yarn-troppo.sense: Terms fit: "the mob in charge of the Mount Vernon estate", "the old girl had a good innings", "a pressie", "a rough trot for the famous old US trees", "Not going in the woodheap, this one."
yarn-troppo.authenticity: Mostly natural ("Not anymore, but.", "a good innings", "a rough trot"), with some stock tags: "Fair dinkum.", "Now, ya might've heard this one."
yarn-troppo.register: Well above level 3: told as a pub yarn with a frame and asides ("That's a bit breezy, I reckon.", "Now here's the bit I like.", "Ya could drive through it, apparently. Not anymore, but."). No swearing.
yarn-troppo.tone: A short news item becomes a chatty, joking yarn: "That's a bit breezy, I reckon." The loss of a historic tree is played more for laughs than the original's neutral report.
yarn-troppo.flow: Reads aloud, but the fragments and lead-ins chop it up: "In a whisky barrel. Fair dinkum." "Ya could drive through it, apparently. Not anymore, but."
yarn-troppo.variety: Highly varied: "whopper", "belted", "the mob", "woodheap", "good innings", "patch", "pressie", "rough trot", "big fella".
yarn-troppo.essence: The facts are all there, but the shape is now a yarn with commentary rather than a brief news report: "Now here's the bit I like."

engine.meaning: The original verbatim apart from one word, so every fact survives: "sent by New York Governor George Clinton as a pressie delivered in a whisky barrel".
engine.sense: The single Aussie word, "a pressie", fits 'gift'.
engine.authenticity: Its one swap sits oddly in untouched wire-service prose: "officials overseeing the Mount Vernon estate indicated", "as a pressie delivered in a whisky barrel", with "110 kph" kept.
engine.register: Essentially untranslated: one word ("pressie") in the whole text, far below level 3.
engine.tone: The neutral news tone is intact, since the text is: "Friday's major winter storm over the northeastern United States claimed a 227-year-old tree".
engine.flow: Reads as the original does, including its awkward "on the estate of the first US President George Washington, Mount Vernon, in Virginia".
engine.essence: Unmistakably the original, being the original.

yarn-dinkum.meaning: All facts survive in order: "a 227-year-old tree at Mount Vernon in Virginia", "gusts of reportedly up to 70 mph (about 110 km/h)", "delivered in a whisky barrel, no less", the Clinton disclaimer and the two other trees. "with bits set aside for special projects" is a fair reading of 'special projects'.
yarn-dinkum.sense: Fits throughout: "has taken out a 227-year-old tree", "The hemlock went in back in 1791" for planted, "Washington's own patch", "the Mount Vernon mob", "to come a gutser lately" for falling.
yarn-dinkum.authenticity: Sounds like an Australian telling the news: "So get this.", "knocked flat", "come a gutser", "cos the first White House wasn't built yet".
yarn-dinkum.register: Level 3: the report retold in a relaxed Aussie voice without asides or jokes beyond "no less". No swearing.
yarn-dinkum.tone: Keeps the news brief's neutral, mildly curious tone: "And no, the New York governor's no relation to the 42nd President Bill Clinton".
yarn-dinkum.flow: Reads like it was written that way: "It's not the only old US tree to come a gutser lately, either."
yarn-dinkum.variety: Good range: "taken out", "knocked flat", "patch", "mob", "pressie", "no less", "come a gutser".
yarn-dinkum.essence: Unmistakably the Mount Vernon hemlock story, its shape as a news item kept.

yarn-deadset.meaning: Complete and accurate: "gusts of reportedly up to 70 mph (about 110 km/h)", "sent by New York Governor George Clinton as a pressie delivered in a whisky barrel".
yarn-deadset.sense: The Aussie it uses fits: "the mob running the Mount Vernon estate", "a pressie", "trees that have come down lately".
yarn-deadset.authenticity: Natural but plain: "Washington's own place", "the Mount Vernon people", "is no relation to".
yarn-deadset.register: Somewhat lighter than level 3: a few words ("mob", "pressie", "knocked over") on otherwise plain news prose.
yarn-deadset.tone: Neutral news tone kept: "The hemlock, planted in 1791, was blown over by gusts".
yarn-deadset.flow: Readable, but keeps the original's stiff joins: "knocked over a 227-year-old tree on the estate of the first US President George Washington, at Mount Vernon in Virginia".

unharnessed.meaning: Complete and accurate, every fact in order: "sent as a gift by New York Governor George Clinton and delivered in a whisky barrel".
unharnessed.sense: What it changes fits: "has taken out a 227-year-old tree", "got knocked over", "trees to come down lately".
unharnessed.authenticity: Natural, idiomatic plain English rather than marked Aussie: "the people running the Mount Vernon estate", "though George Clinton did go on to become"; "110 kph" kept.
unharnessed.register: Lighter than level 3: barely any Australian vocabulary beyond "taken out" and "knocked over".
unharnessed.tone: Neutral news tone kept: "Friday's big winter storm across the north-east of the United States has taken out".
unharnessed.flow: Smooth, and it fixes the original's clunky opening: "a 227-year-old tree at Mount Vernon, the Virginia estate of the first US President, George Washington".
unharnessed.variety: Very little to vary: "taken out", "knocked over", "come down".
